'''Tristram Chivers''' (born 22 August 1940) is a British-Canadian chemist and Professor Emeritus at the [[University of Calgary]]. His main research interest is the inorganic chemistry of [[Main-group element|the main group elements]], particularly [[boron]], [[nitrogen]], [[phosphorus]], [[sulfur]], [[selenium]], and [[tellurium]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Tristram Chivers |url=https://profiles.ucalgary.ca/tristram-chivers |website=University of Calgary |access-date=23 May 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

Chivers was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada]] in 1991 and is also a Fellow of the [[Chemical Institute of Canada]]. He has been described as the "godfather" of main group chemistry in Canada.<ref name="burford">{{cite journal |last=Burford |first=Neil |title=This special issue is dedicated to Professor Tristram Chivers |journal=Canadian Journal of Chemistry |volume=80 |issue=11 |pages=x–xiv |date=November 2002 |doi=10.1139/v02-904}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Chivers, Dr. Tristram |url=https://astech.ca/archives/indexofpastwinners/chivers-dr-tristram |website=ASTech Awards |publisher=ASTech Foundation |access-date=23 May 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
 |title=Complete List of CIC Fellows
 |url=https://www.cheminst.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Complete-List-of-CIC-Fellows-20260407.pdf
 |website=Chemical Institute of Canada
 |publisher=Chemical Institute of Canada
 |date=2026-04-07
 |format=PDF
 |access-date=2026-05-23
}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Chivers was born in [[Bath, Somerset]] and attended [[Colston's School]] in [[Bristol]]. He graduated from [[Durham University]] in 1961 with a [[first-class honours|first-class]] degree in chemistry.<ref name=burford /> 

He stayed on at Durham for doctoral studies, and completed his PhD in 1964 under the supervision of [[Richard Dickinson Chambers|R. D. Chambers]].<ref name=burford /><ref>{{cite thesis |last=Chivers |first=Tristram |title=Some pentafluorophenyl derivatives of tin and boron |access-date=21 May 2025 |type=PhD thesis |publisher=Durham University |url=https://etheses.dur.ac.uk/8909/1/8909_5840.PDF?UkUDh:CyT |year=1964}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Doctor of Science#United Kingdom, Ireland, India, Pakistan and the Commonwealth|DSc degree]] by Durham University in 1981.<ref name="burford" />

==Career and research==
After brief periods as a [[postdoc]] at the [[University of Cincinnati]] and a tutorial fellow at the [[University of Sussex]], Chivers moved permanently to Canada in 1967, joining the [[University of British Columbia]] as a teaching postdoctoral fellow. In 1969, he joined the [[University of Calgary]] as an assistant professor, becoming a full professor in 1978.<ref name=burford /><ref>{{cite web |title=Meet the donors |url=https://ucalgary.ca/news/meet-donors-spark-fall-2024 |website=University of Calgary |access-date=23 May 2025 |language=en |date=30 August 2024}}</ref> He served as head of the Department of Chemistry from 1977 to 1982.<ref name=burford />

At Calgary, Chivers and his colleagues made "notable contributions" to the chemistry of [[chalcogen#compounds|chalcogen compounds]]. His early work included identifying the blue species formed by sulfur in reducing media as the trisulfur radical anion, which was subsequently shown by [[Robin Clark (chemist)|Robin Clark]] to be the blue chromophore in the mineral [[lapis lazuli]].<ref name=burford /> Several ring and cage compounds discovered by Chivers and his collaborators became "textbook examples"; the 1998 edition of ''Chemistry of the Elements'' by [[Norman Greenwood]] and Alan Earnshaw devoted twelve pages to sulfur–nitrogen chemistry originating from his laboratory.<ref name=burford />

Chivers was senior editor of the ''[[Canadian Journal of Chemistry]]'' from 1993 to 1998 and served as president of the Canadian Society for Chemistry (CSC) from 2000 to 2001.<ref name=burford />

He received the E. W. R. Steacie Award from the [[Canadian Society for Chemistry]] in 2001 and an [[honorary degree]] from the [[University of Oulu]] in Finland in 2006.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cheminst.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/CSC-E.-W.-R.-Steacie-Award-Previous-Recipients-20251202.pdf |title=E. W. R. Steacie Award: List of Recipients |publisher=Chemical Institute of Canada |access-date=8 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.oulu.fi/en/conferment-ceremony/previous-honorary-doctors |title=Previous Honorary Doctors |publisher=University of Oulu |access-date=8 May 2026}}</ref> In 2025, he received the Wolfgang Günther Award for Lifetime Achievement in Selenium and Tellurium Chemistry.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.iccst.org/ |title=International Conferences on the Chemistry of Selenium & Tellurium |publisher=ICCST |access-date=8 May 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260218084259/https://www.iccst.org/ |archive-date=18 February 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
